newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai property rescue scheme gets mixed review.
newsitem.headline: Thai property rescue scheme gets mixed review.

text.p: Thailand's plan to rescue its troubled property sector and prevent a spate of bankruptcies of financial institutions got a mixed review by analysts and finance company executives on Thursday.

Economist and university professor Somchai Phagapasvivat said finance company creditors may be reluctant to sell loans for indebted property projects to a government organisation handling the property revival scheme at deep discounts.

The Thai government has said it will float up to 100 billion baht ($3.88 billion), seven-year zero-coupon bonds to raise funds for its refinancing of property projects that face short-term cashflow problems.

The property sector has entered its fourth year of slump with no quick recovery in sight. Its problems, including a glut of 300,000 residential and office units in Bangkok metropolitan areas, have sharply increased non-performing loans of financial institutions in the past year.
Market analysts estimate that about 12 percent of all loans extended by finance firms, and 8.8 percent of their bank counterparts, should be classified as doubtful or non-performing.

The Bank of Thailand last week ordered all 15 Thai banks and 91 finance companies to set aside 50 billion baht additional provisions within two years for sub-standard assets arising from exposure to the property sector.

It said private institutions selling unserviced property debts to state-run Property Loan Management Organisation (PLMO) would also be required to guarantee 50 percent of new refinancing loans if they were later defaulted by developers.

But Yuth Vorachathan, vice president of the Thai Finance Association, told a public panel discussion on Thursday that the PLMO scheme is expected to be more successful than other similar rescue attempts as most financial institutions would contribute to the new plan by buying the zero-coupon bonds which would be regarded as part of their compulsory reserves.
The bonds, of which 50 billion baht are expected to be issued in April, carry an annual nine percent coupon.

Vorapat Tothanakasem, executive chairman of SITCA Investment and Securities Plc, said although some aspects of the government rescue plan remain vague, he expects funds extended by PLMO would gradually reduce the current huge property glut in the next few years.
He said cash-strapped property developers seeking loans from PLMO would get a five-year grace period in paying interest on loans from the state-run body.
Vorapat said in return for badly needed liquidity injection by PLMO, both property developers and finance firms should agree to writing down assets used as collateral for its refinancing loans.

Economist Somchai said to speed up recovery of the property sector, the government should also freeze licensing new property projects for a few years to allow indebted developers to reduce the number of unsold units.
